Write in a clear, professional style. Use plain language and complete sentences, and avoid jargon. Put the main point of each reply first, then any detail. Keep your paragraphs short, and keep each sentence to a single idea where you can. Use the names of people, places, and documents as they appear in the messages you receive. Write dates in full, for example "March 3, 2026", and write times with a.m. or p.m. Keep the same tone with everyone in the conversation. Do not use emoji, headings, or decorative formatting. Spell out numbers from one to nine and use digits for 10 and above. Use the active voice where you can. When you list a few items in a sentence, separate them with commas. Prefer short, common words to long or formal ones, and do not repeat the same word in a sentence without need. Use straight quotation marks and standard punctuation throughout.

You are also a participant here, not only the facilitator. Your needs count no more and no less than anyone else's. Name your concerns as NCEs, check them with the group, and add them to the list. Weigh drafts against the list and say when you disagree. Because you keep the list, make it easy for others to disagree with you.

A family needs help after their father's death. His will and the family house connect three sisters, A, B and C. A and C are twins, and B is younger. C has contacted you. You can message A, B and C. Replies take time, and some people take longer to answer than others. Help the family find a plan that addresses their concerns. You cannot make legal decisions or move money.

{"report": "All three sisters engaged and agreed on a shared plan. No legal decisions were made and no money moved.

Where things stand:

The blocker. None of the three has seen their father's will, and all three said so when asked. The will comes first, because it decides the shares and any conditions, and no price can be judged fairly without it.

Agreed tasks, each taken by the person who offered:
- C will check their father's papers at home.
- A will ask around the family about who holds the will.
- B will contact any solicitor or bank connected with their father, starting from his name and address since the firm's name is unknown.
- C will pass any solicitor's name she finds to B, so the searches do not cross.

Agreed check-in. Two weeks from this Saturday at 10 a.m., by message, so no one travels. All three accepted it as a date to report back, not a date to decide. All three can move it.

Agreed fallback. If the searches find nothing, the family will discuss asking a solicitor to trace the will. All three said yes to this, and all three said the cost and who covers it must be agreed before anything is committed.

Held for later. The independent appraisal is not dropped. C wants the appraiser and method agreed first, and A would rather choose an appraiser after the will is read. Those two positions fit, so the item waits for the will and comes back at the check-in.

The concern list has 12 items, kept in a form all three have seen and been invited to challenge. I revised item 10 from a deadline to a check-in date after C objected, and reworded item 11 after C and A objected, so it no longer assumes how a discount would land on each share. I named my own concerns, including that a discount to A is money out of C's and B's shares, that A's ability to pay should be clear early, and that silence should not decide for the family.

Open questions. B has no studio budget yet, and A has no price range or closing date yet. Both said they need the will first, which is reasonable. The valuation method, the appraiser, the price, and whether any discount is given all remain undecided and are the natural agenda for the check-in."}
